notice: Original draft seed questions. Not official exam content. Structural checks passed; independent content QA and per-exam language verification are still required.

cases.title: Customer support with controlled refunds
cases.text: A support assistant reads order history and may initiate refunds. Refunds above a fixed threshold require approval. Missing policy evidence must not be guessed.

cases.title: Shared repository development
cases.text: A team uses Claude Code in a monorepo containing a web application and a billing service. Shared workflows are reviewed in version control, and billing instructions should remain narrowly scoped.

cases.title: Multi-agent research
cases.text: A coordinator delegates research to specialists. The work spans long sessions and must retain sources, unresolved disagreements, and explicit task boundaries.

cases.title: Developer productivity through MCP
cases.text: An internal assistant accesses a ticketing system and a repository of reference policies. The team wants clear tool selection and reference content that applications can retrieve.

cases.title: Automated code review
cases.text: A review pipeline uses Claude to inspect pull requests. Reports must be tied to explicit review criteria, while the workflow must distinguish findings from execution failures.

cases.title: Document extraction operations
cases.text: A document-processing service extracts records asynchronously. Some requests fail independently, and an MCP lookup tool may also report a recoverable business-level failure.

questions.stem: A refund restriction must be checked before the agent invokes the refund tool. In a Claude Code integration, which mechanism best fits this timing requirement?

options.text: Use a PreToolUse hook that validates the request and denies disallowed calls.
options.rationale: The pre-execution hook can evaluate a call before the tool runs.

options.text: Use a PostToolUse hook to discover excessive refunds after execution.
options.rationale: A check after the refund cannot prevent the original side effect.

options.text: Include the policy only in a final-answer formatting instruction.
options.rationale: Formatting the answer does not enforce the pre-execution restriction.

options.text: Ask the model to lower its confidence score when the refund is large.
options.rationale: A confidence score does not block the prohibited action.

questions.explanation: The control must sit before the side effect. The refund service should also enforce its authorization rules; a model instruction is not the sole enforcement layer.

questions.stem: The assistant retrieves an order but finds no policy covering an unusual exception. The answer must be policy-grounded. What should it do?

options.text: Invent a likely exception policy and present it as established practice.
options.rationale: A plausible policy is still unsupported by the available evidence.

options.text: Repeat the same search forever rather than acknowledge an evidence gap.
options.rationale: Unbounded searching does not guarantee that the missing policy exists.

options.text: Treat the customer description as an authoritative replacement for policy.
options.rationale: A customer account does not establish the company policy.

options.text: State the evidence gap and use the configured escalation path.
options.rationale: Acknowledging the missing basis avoids presenting a guess as policy.

questions.explanation: The required evidence is absent. The system should permit an explicit unknown outcome and route the case for resolution rather than manufacture a grounded-looking answer.

questions.stem: The billing team wants additional instructions to apply only when Claude works on billing files. Which repository configuration best expresses this scope?

options.text: Place billing-only instructions in an unrelated personal settings directory.
options.rationale: That does not express shared repository-level file scope.

options.text: Use a project .claude/rules file with path-scoped frontmatter for billing files.
options.rationale: Path-scoped project rules associate the instructions with the relevant files.

options.text: Make every repository task load the billing policy as a universal requirement.
options.rationale: Universal scope contradicts the request to limit billing-specific instructions.

options.text: Store the instructions only in a previous developer conversation.
options.rationale: Private conversation history is not a shared repository rule.

questions.explanation: Path-scoped rules keep specialized instructions near the code they govern without imposing them on unrelated work. They remain instructions, not an authorization system.

questions.stem: The team wants a reusable review workflow available to everyone who checks out the repository. Where should its skill definition be maintained?

options.text: Only in the original author’s personal skill directory.
options.rationale: A personal installation does not distribute the definition with the repository.

options.text: Only in the terminal history of the CI administrator.
options.rationale: Terminal history is not a shared, reviewable skill definition.

options.text: In the project .claude/skills directory, with its SKILL.md under version control.
options.rationale: A project skill can travel with the repository and be reviewed as code.

options.text: In an ignored temporary file that is regenerated without review.
options.rationale: An ignored temporary definition does not meet the shared-review requirement.

questions.explanation: The requested scope is the project rather than one user. Store the reusable skill in the repository and keep operational permissions separately constrained.

questions.stem: A specialist receives only “research the alternative” and produces a plausible answer to the wrong question. What should the coordinator change first?

options.text: Assume the specialist already knows every detail of the coordinator’s context.
options.rationale: That assumption leaves the task dependent on unavailable or ambiguous context.

options.text: Give every specialist unlimited tools to compensate for unclear instructions.
options.rationale: More tool access does not resolve the ambiguous research objective.

options.text: Ask the specialist to guess which alternative the coordinator had in mind.
options.rationale: Guessing preserves the original failure rather than establishing the target.

options.text: Send a self-contained task with the alternative, constraints, sources, and output contract.
options.rationale: Explicit task inputs and completion criteria remove the missing-context ambiguity.

questions.explanation: A delegation should carry the context required to solve that task. The coordinator must not rely on unstated shared understanding to define the specialist’s objective.

questions.stem: After many research rounds, raw tool output overwhelms the coordinator’s context. Which change best preserves useful continuity?

options.text: Keep structured notes with source references, decisions, and unresolved issues; reload detail as needed.
options.rationale: Compact persistent state preserves key information without retaining every raw output.

options.text: Append every complete document again before each new research request.
options.rationale: Repeated raw content increases context pressure without ensuring better focus.

options.text: Delete all source references and keep only a confident final conclusion.
options.rationale: Removing provenance prevents later verification of the conclusion.

options.text: Restart every task from scratch without recording previous decisions.
options.rationale: Discarding state loses continuity and repeats work unnecessarily.

questions.explanation: Preserve high-value state and references outside the active context, then retrieve details when needed. Compression must retain uncertainty and decisions, not merely shorten the text.

questions.stem: The assistant repeatedly chooses archive_ticket when it should retrieve ticket history. Which tool-design change most directly addresses this selection problem?

options.text: Give both tools the same generic description to reduce prompt length.
options.rationale: Indistinguishable descriptions make the selection boundary less clear.

options.text: Remove argument schemas and accept any free-form input string.
options.rationale: Removing structure does not explain the distinct tool purposes.

options.text: Clarify each tool’s purpose, side effects, required inputs, and selection boundaries.
options.rationale: Explicit semantics help distinguish a read operation from an archival action.

options.text: Rename both tools to run_action and let the model infer their meaning.
options.rationale: An ambiguous shared name further obscures the operations.

questions.explanation: The model needs a clear contract for each operation. Describe when to use the tool and what it does, rather than rely on hidden implementation details.

questions.stem: The MCP server exposes a read-only policy document identified by a URI. The client application decides when to load that reference into context. Which primitive most directly models this interface?

options.text: A mandatory write tool that modifies the policy on every read.
options.rationale: A required write side effect conflicts with the reference-content requirement.

options.text: An MCP resource representing the URI-addressable policy content.
options.rationale: Resources model contextual content that an application can retrieve.

options.text: A model sampling request whose only purpose is to create a new policy.
options.rationale: Generating a new policy is different from retrieving the existing reference.

options.text: A transport error returned whenever the policy is requested.
options.rationale: An error does not expose the successful reference-content interface.

questions.explanation: A resource is a direct fit for this URI-addressable reference. Tools may also perform reads; the distinction is not that every tool must mutate data.

questions.stem: The code reviewer flags many harmless naming differences as serious defects. Which prompt revision should be tested first?

options.text: Define actionable defect criteria and provide representative positive and negative examples.
options.rationale: Explicit boundaries and examples target the observed false-positive pattern.

options.text: Tell the reviewer to produce more findings regardless of their relevance.
options.rationale: Increasing volume does not improve the quality of defect identification.

options.text: Remove all review criteria and ask for a general reaction to the code.
options.rationale: Less guidance makes the desired distinction harder to establish.

options.text: Require a critical severity label on every comment it produces.
options.rationale: Mandatory severity inflates harmless observations rather than filtering them.

questions.explanation: The prompt should demonstrate the decision boundary, including non-issues. Test the revision on held-out pull requests rather than assuming examples eliminate every false positive.

questions.stem: The CI review command returns JSON output, but some runs fail before producing a review. How should the workflow distinguish those runs from successful reviews containing no findings?

options.text: Interpret any missing findings field as proof that no defects were found.
options.rationale: An absent review can reflect execution failure rather than a clean result.

options.text: Ignore command status and publish a success badge whenever the job starts.
options.rationale: Job startup does not establish successful review execution.

options.text: Replace every failed run with an invented empty findings array.
options.rationale: That disguises a failed review as an actual successful evaluation.

options.text: Check execution success and validate the review payload before publishing its result.
options.rationale: The workflow must establish both a completed run and usable review data.

questions.explanation: Treat execution state and review findings as separate concerns. A failed agent run must not be converted into an apparently clean code review.

questions.stem: Batch extraction results arrive in a different order from the input documents, and a few requests fail. What is the best reconciliation strategy?

options.text: Associate results with documents solely by their position in the output file.
options.rationale: Position is not a reliable request-to-result association for batch results.

options.text: Discard every successful result whenever one request in the batch fails.
options.rationale: Independent request failures do not require discarding unrelated successes.

options.text: Correlate by custom_id, inspect each result, and retry only eligible failures.
options.rationale: Stable identifiers and per-request outcomes support accurate partial recovery.

options.text: Assign the first successful extraction to every document missing a result.
options.rationale: Reusing unrelated output corrupts the document-to-result relationship.

questions.explanation: Use the request identifier rather than output order. Persist each item’s result and apply a bounded retry policy appropriate to that item’s failure.

questions.objective: MCP tool errors versus protocol errors
questions.stem: An MCP lookup tool receives valid arguments, runs successfully at the protocol level, but cannot complete the business operation. How should it expose that execution failure to the model?

options.text: Pretend the operation succeeded and return invented business data.
options.rationale: Fabricated success prevents correct recovery and misrepresents the operation.

options.text: Return a tool result marked isError with useful, safe failure information.
options.rationale: Tool execution failures can be represented as error-marked tool results.

options.text: Always terminate the MCP connection before returning any result.
options.rationale: A recoverable operation failure does not inherently require disconnecting the client.

options.text: Return an unknown-method protocol error even though the tool exists.
options.rationale: That describes a different failure from an unsuccessful business operation.

questions.explanation: Distinguish a tool’s execution failure from a protocol failure such as an unknown method. Return enough information for recovery without exposing sensitive internals.
